name: Losar in Lachung and Lachen
when: February or early March (first days of the first Tibetan month)
summary: Losar, the Tibetan New Year, is the main winter festival in the Bhutia villages of Lachung and Lachen. It is mainly a family and monastery occasion, with prayers, new prayer flags and visits between households.
body: Losar falls on the first day of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February and sometimes in early March. In Lachung and Lachen families clean their houses, hang new prayer flags, prepare special food and visit the monastery. Celebrations continue for several days with visits between relatives and friends.

It is not a staged tourist event. Most of the festival happens in homes and at the monasteries, and some families travel down to Gangtok or Mangan for the winter. If you are in the valleys at Losar, you may see prayers at the monastery and villagers in their best traditional dress.
Winter travel brings its own problems: snow can close roads above Lachung, and some hotels and homestays close for the holiday. Check with your operator that your stay will be open.
tips: Confirm that your hotel or homestay is open over Losar.
Ask before photographing people or prayers at the monastery.
Dress for snow and keep a spare day in your plan.
A small gift of fruit or sweets is a kind gesture if you are invited into a home.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated in North Sikkim?
faqs.a: Losar follows the Tibetan lunar calendar and usually falls in February, occasionally early March. Exact dates change each year. Check the date for your year with your operator or the Sikkim tourism calendar before you plan around it. Celebrations usually run for several days after the first day of the new year.

Visitors can watch prayers at the monasteries and may be invited into homes, especially if staying in a homestay. It is a family festival, so behave as a guest, ask before photographing and do not expect performances. A homestay is the best way to see how local families mark the new year.

faqs.q: Are roads to Lachung open at Losar?
faqs.a: Usually the road to Lachung is open, but snow can close it for a day or more, and the road above to Zero Point often closes after snowfall. Keep a spare day. Check current status before you travel. Some hotels also close for the holiday, so confirm your booking.

faqs.q: Is Losar the same as Losoong?
faqs.a: No. Losoong is the Sikkimese harvest New Year, celebrated in December with masked dances at monasteries such as Rumtek. Losar is the Tibetan New Year in February or March. Both are important in Sikkim and are often confused. Lachung and Lachen mark Losar mainly at home and in their monasteries.

name: Saga Dawa at Lachen Monastery
when: May or June (full moon of the fourth Tibetan month)
summary: Saga Dawa marks the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha and is observed across Sikkim, including at the monasteries of Lachen and Lachung. Villagers gather for prayers, butter lamps and processions with scriptures.
body: Saga Dawa falls on the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, usually in late May or June. Buddhists in Sikkim treat the whole month as a time for merit: many avoid meat, give alms and visit monasteries. On the main day, monks and villagers carry holy texts around the village in procession.

In Gangtok the procession is large and public. In Lachen and Lachung it is smaller and more local, centred on the village monastery. If you are in North Sikkim at that time, you may see villagers walking with scriptures, lighting lamps and praying.
Saga Dawa comes at the start of the monsoon, when landslides may close roads and permits can be suspended. Do not plan a trip solely around it without a backup plan.
tips: Dress modestly and walk clockwise around monasteries and stupas.
Do not walk in front of a procession or interrupt prayers for photos.
Avoid meat and alcohol in public on the day out of respect.
Keep two spare days for monsoon road closures.

faqs.a: Saga Dawa is the holiest Buddhist observance in Sikkim, marking the birth, enlightenment and passing of the Buddha. It falls on the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, usually late May or June. It is a state holiday in Sikkim, with prayers and processions in monasteries.

faqs.q: Where is the biggest Saga Dawa celebration?
faqs.a: The largest public procession is in Gangtok. In North Sikkim, villages such as Lachen and Lachung mark the day at their own monasteries with prayers, lamps and smaller processions. These are local events rather than tourist shows. If you are in Gangtok on the day, the procession through town is well worth seeing.

faqs.q: Is it a good time to travel to North Sikkim?
faqs.a: It can be, if roads are open. Late May is still good weather, but by June the monsoon may cause landslides and permit suspensions. Keep spare days and a backup plan in lower Sikkim. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I take photos during Saga Dawa?
faqs.a: Photography of processions outdoors is usually accepted from a respectful distance. Inside monastery halls, ask first and do not use flash. Never stand in front of monks or block the procession to take pictures. Ask people before taking close portraits, and put the camera away during prayers if asked.

name: Namsoong, the Lepcha New Year
when: December, around the start of the Lepcha month of Kurnyit
summary: Namsoong is the Lepcha New Year, celebrated by Lepcha families in Dzongu and across Sikkim and Kalimpong in December. It mixes household rites, traditional food, songs and dances, with bigger public events in Gangtok.
body: Namsoong marks the Lepcha New Year and the end of the harvest. Lepcha tradition links it to the defeat of a demon, Laso Mung, and the return of light. Families clean their homes, prepare food and chi, the millet beer, and gather for rituals and celebrations.

In Dzongu it is a community and family occasion. Larger public celebrations with stalls, dances and songs are usually held in Gangtok and in Kalimpong. If you stay in a Dzongu homestay around Namsoong, your hosts may share the festival with you.
December is dry, cool and clear in Dzongu, so it is a good time for a village stay. Ask your host about exact dates, which follow the Lepcha calendar.
tips: Ask your homestay host about dates a few weeks ahead.
Accept or politely decline chi; no one will mind either way.
Wear modest, warm clothes for evening gatherings.
Ask before photographing rituals or people in traditional dress.

faqs.a: Namsoong falls in December, at the start of the Lepcha month of Kurnyit, and celebrations can run for several days, sometimes into early January in public events. The exact dates follow the Lepcha calendar. Ask your Dzongu host or check Gangtok event listings.

The largest public celebrations are usually in Gangtok and Kalimpong, with dances, songs and food stalls. In Dzongu it is mostly a family and village event. Staying with a Lepcha homestay is the best way to see how families celebrate.

faqs.q: What is the story behind Namsoong?
faqs.a: Lepcha tradition tells of a demon king, Laso Mung, who brought darkness and suffering until he was defeated, and Namsoong celebrates that victory and the new year. Your hosts may tell the story in their own version. The festival also marks the end of the harvest and a time for families to gather.

faqs.q: Is December a good time to visit Dzongu?
faqs.a: Yes. Dzongu sits low enough to stay pleasant in December, with cool, clear days and cold nights. It is dry, leech-free and good for walking. You can pair it with a snowy night or two in Lachung. Pack warm layers for the evenings, as homestays are rarely heated.
